mainTopic: Burning on שבת without needing the ashes (רבי יוחנן), the clever-ox and רבא answers, and the new משנה about chasing oxen and the burden of proof.
overview: The גמרא is testing רבי יוחנן's view that burning on שבת is only punishable when the person needs the ashes. A proof from the משנה says the person who set a fire is like the ox who set a fire, and the ox surely did not need the ashes. The גמרא flips the comparison: the ox's case is like the person's, so the ox also needed the ashes. רב אויא describes a clever ox with a bite on its back. It burned a haystack to roll in the ashes, and we know this because it really rolled in them afterward. The story of רב פפא's ox, which cured its toothache by drinking beer, shows that oxen can act this way. The חכמים challenge the idea that the ox matches the person from the case of embarrassment (בושת). The גמרא answers that intending to injure is enough to make someone liable for embarrassment. רבא offers another answer: the משנה is about a fire set by mistake (בשוגג). Based on the teaching of דבי חזקיה, an act that brings death when done on purpose frees a person from paying even when it was done by mistake. A new משנה then begins about an ox that was chasing another ox, ruling that the one who wants to collect must bring proof. It then starts the case of two chasing oxen whose owners blame each other, and the ruling for that case comes on the next amud.

steps.title: Finishing the proof: the person's case, like the ox's, did not need the ashes
steps.stepSummary: The ox's case and the person's case in the משנה are parallel. The ox did not need the ashes, so the person also did not need them. Yet the משנה calls him a capital sinner, which shows burning on שבת counts even without needing the ashes.
steps.simpleTranslation: So too, he (the person) did not need the ashes. And still the משנה teaches that he is exempt from paying because he is liable to death.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes a proof against רבי יוחנן. Since the person's case is like the ox's, he too did not need the ashes, yet the משנה says he is liable to death for burning on שבת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה exempts him from paying only because he gets the death penalty for breaking שבת. That means his burning counted as a real שבת violation. If he did not need the ashes, then destructive burning is still punishable, against רבי יוחנן.

keyTerms.meaning: He does not need it (the ashes)
He is judged with his life, meaning he is liable to the death penalty
Exempt (here, from paying for the haystack)

steps.confusionAlert: פָּטוּר here does not mean he did nothing wrong. He is exempt from paying money only because he deserves a much harsher punishment, death, for breaking שבת.

phrases.aramaic: אַף הוּא נָמֵי דְּלָא קָבָעֵי לֵיהּ;
phrases.english: so too he, where he does not need it;
phrases.notes: 'He' is the person who set the fire himself. 'It' means the ashes.

phrases.english: and it teaches: exempt –
because he is sentenced with his life!

steps.triggerLanguage: אַף הוּא נָמֵי דְּלָא קָבָעֵי לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes a proof that began just before this section, comparing the person's case to the ox's case.
steps.raayaObject: That burning on שבת is punishable even when the burner does not need the ashes, against רבי יוחנן.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה, which exempts the person from paying because he is liable to death, read as parallel to the ox who did not need the ashes.

steps.title: Reversing the comparison: the ox's case is like the person's
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof. The person's case is the base, and he needed the ashes, so the ox's case must also be one where the ox needed the ashes.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. His ox is like him. Just as he needed the ashes, so too his ox needed the ashes.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the proof by flipping which case explains which.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof assumed the ox's case sets the terms for the person's case. The גמרא says the reverse: the person needed the ashes, as רבי יוחנן requires, and the ox's case matches him. So the משנה gives no proof against רבי יוחנן.

keyTerms.meaning: Just as ... so too (a parallel comparison)

steps.whyThisMatters: This keeps רבי יוחנן's rule in place: burning on שבת is only liable when the ashes are needed.

phrases.english: No; his ox is similar to him –
just as he is where he needs it,
so too his ox is where it needs it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof from step 1 by flipping the direction of the comparison.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The whole proof from the משנה.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: It assumed the ox's case explains the person's case. It could just as well be the other way around.

steps.title: How can an ox need ashes?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how we could ever find an ox that sets a fire because it needs the ashes.
steps.simpleTranslation: With his ox, how can you find such a case?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the rejection it just gave. It sets up the next step by asking how an ox could need ashes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The new reading only works if a real case exists where an ox burns something for the ashes. An animal does not normally plan like that, so the גמרא asks for a realistic case.

keyTerms.meaning: How can you find it? (asking for a realistic case)

phrases.english: His ox – how can you find it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions whether the case described in step 2 can really happen.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A realistic case in which an ox burns something because it needs the ashes.

steps.title: רב אויא: a clever ox with a bite on its back
steps.stepSummary: רב אויא says the case is an intelligent ox that was bitten on its back. It wanted to burn the haystack and roll in the ashes.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אויא said to him: Here we are dealing with a clever ox that had a bite on its back. It wanted to burn the haystack and roll around in the ashes.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אויא answers the question by describing a real case where an ox needs ashes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A clever ox with a wound has a reason to want ashes: rolling in them helps the bite. So the ox's burning can be 'for the ashes,' just like the person's, and the reading from step 2 holds.

keyTerms.meaning: Here, what are we dealing with? (introduces a specific case)

phrases.english: Rav Avya said to him:
Here, with what are we dealing –
with an intelligent ox that developed
a bite on its back,
and it wants to burn it
and roll around in the ashes.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אַוְיָא: הָכָא בְּמַאי עָסְקִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 3's question with a specific case.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A clever ox with a bite on its back burns the haystack so it can roll in the ashes to treat the wound.

steps.title: How do we know why the ox did it?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how we could know that the ox burned the haystack for the ashes.
steps.simpleTranslation: And from where do we know?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks how anyone could tell what the ox intended. This sets up the final answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An ox cannot tell us its reasons. The גמרא needs some visible sign that the burning was done for the ashes.

phrases.english: And from where do we know?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks how we can know the ox's purpose described in step 4.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Evidence that the ox burned the haystack in order to use the ashes.

steps.title: Because the ox rolled in the ashes afterward
steps.stepSummary: We know the ox's purpose because after it burned the haystack, it rolled around in the ashes.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because after it burned the haystack, it was rolling around in the ashes.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers: the ox's own behavior afterward shows why it set the fire.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Rolling in the ashes right after the fire shows the ox wanted them. So the ox's case fits needing the ashes, and the משנה stays consistent with רבי יוחנן.
steps.whatToRemember: The משנה does not disprove רבי יוחנן. Both the person and the ox are cases of needing the ashes: a clever, wounded ox burned the haystack and then rolled in the ashes.

phrases.english: Because after it burned it
it was rolling around in the ashes.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 5 and completes the defense of רבי יוחנן.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The ox's behavior after the fire, rolling in the ashes, shows it burned the haystack for the ashes.

steps.title: Is there really such a smart ox?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether an ox could really act with such a clear purpose.
steps.simpleTranslation: And is there really a case like this?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pauses to ask whether this situation can actually happen. Can an ox be clever enough to burn a haystack on purpose so it can roll in the ashes?
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב אויא's answer depends on an animal acting with a real plan. Before the גמרא accepts that, it wants to know whether animals ever really behave this way.

keyTerms.meaning: And is there really…? (doubting whether something exists)
Like this, in this kind of way

phrases.english: And is there really a case like this?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions whether the case of the intelligent ox from steps 4–6 is realistic.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether an animal can actually act with purposeful, healing-seeking intelligence.

steps.title: רב פפא's ox that cured its own toothache
steps.stepSummary: Yes. רב פפא's ox had a toothache, broke open a container of beer, drank it, and got better.
steps.simpleTranslation: Yes. There was an ox in רב פפא's house that had a toothache. It went in, broke open the container, drank the beer, and was cured.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers yes and brings a real story as proof. An ox in רב פפא's house treated its own toothache by drinking beer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This story shows that an ox can do something on purpose to cure itself. If an ox can do that, then an ox could also burn a haystack on purpose to soothe a bite by rolling in the ashes.

phrases.english: Yes;

phrases.aramaic: דְּהָהוּא תּוֹרָא דַּהֲוָה בֵּי רַב פָּפָּא
phrases.english: for there was a certain ox in the house of רב פפא
that had a toothache,
it went in and broke open the container,
phrases.notes: נזייתא is a container of drink. The ox broke it open to get to the beer inside.

phrases.english: and drank the beer and was cured.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִין; דְּהָהוּא תּוֹרָא דַּהֲוָה בֵּי רַב פָּפָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 7 with a real-life story about an ox.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Yes. רב פפא's ox deliberately drank beer to cure its toothache, which shows that oxen can act with purpose.

steps.title: The embarrassment case shows the ox and the person cannot match
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים challenge רב פפא: the משנה makes a person liable for embarrassment but exempts his ox. An ox never intends to embarrass, so how can the ox's case match the person's?
steps.simpleTranslation: The חכמים said before רב פפא: How can you say that the ox's case is like the person's case? The משנה teaches: if his ox embarrassed someone, he is exempt, but if he himself embarrassed someone, he is liable. If the ox's case is like the person's, how could you ever find an ox that intended to embarrass?
steps.whatsHappening: The חכמים attack the whole idea that the ox's case in the משנה must be the same as the person's case. They point to another line in the משנה about embarrassment (בושת).
steps.deeperAnalysis: A person only pays for embarrassment when he meant to embarrass. An ox never has that kind of intention. So in the embarrassment case, the ox's situation cannot match the person's, and that seems to break the rule of 'his ox is like him.'

keyTerms.meaning: Similar to him, matching his case
How can you find such a case?

steps.confusionAlert: This challenge is not saying the ox cannot be smart. It is saying the 'ox matches the person' rule seems impossible in the embarrassment case, because an ox can never intend to embarrass.

phrases.english: The חכמים said before רב פפא:

phrases.aramaic: מִי מָצֵית אָמְרַתְּ שׁוֹרוֹ דּוּמְיָא דִידֵיהּ?!
phrases.english: Can you really say that his ox is like him?!
But doesn't it teach:
if his ox embarrassed someone, he is exempt,
and if he himself embarrassed someone, he is liable.
If his ox is like him,
an ox that intended to embarrass, how could you find such a case?

steps.triggerLanguage: מִי מָצֵית אָמְרַתְּ שׁוֹרוֹ דּוּמְיָא דִידֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Now that the intelligent-ox case has been shown to be possible, the חכמים challenge the basic idea that the ox's case must match the person's.
steps.kashyaTarget: The principle that the ox's case in the משנה matches the person's case (שורו דומיא דידיה).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: In the embarrassment ruling, the person is liable only when he intends to embarrass. An ox cannot have that intention, so the two cases cannot match.

steps.title: Intending to injure is enough to be liable for embarrassment
steps.stepSummary: The case is one where the ox meant to hurt someone. A person who means to injure is liable for embarrassment even if he did not mean to embarrass.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is a case where it intended to injure. As the Master said: if one intended to injure, he is liable for embarrassment even though he did not intend to embarrass.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends the 'ox matches the person' idea. The matching case is one where the ox meant to injure, not to embarrass.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An established rule says that a person who meant to injure pays for embarrassment even without meaning to embarrass. An ox can mean to hurt someone, so the two cases match. The person would pay for the embarrassment, while the owner of the ox is exempt.

keyTerms.meaning: For example, it is a case where

steps.whatToRemember: A person who intends to injure is liable for embarrassment (בושת) even if he did not intend to embarrass. That is why the ox's case can still match the person's case.

phrases.english: It is a case where it intended to injure.
As the Master said:
If one intended to injure,
phrases.notes: The words 'he is liable for embarrassment' are left out here, but they are understood.

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁלֹּא נִתְכַּוֵּון לְבַיֵּישׁ.
phrases.english: even though he did not intend to embarrass.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 9 by redefining which case of embarrassment the משנה means.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case (אוקימתא), supported by a known rule
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Liability for embarrassment needs intent to embarrass, which an ox can never have.
steps.terutzMaskana: Intent to injure is enough for liability for embarrassment. An ox can intend to injure, so its case can match the person's.

steps.title: רבא: the משנה is talking about acting by mistake
steps.stepSummary: רבא opens a different explanation: the משנה's case of someone who set a fire on שבת is one where he did it by mistake.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: The משנה is talking about someone who acted by mistake.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא begins a completely new way of explaining the משנה. This line sets up his approach, which steps 12–14 fill in.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא answers the challenge against רבי יוחנן from step 1 without needing the clever-ox explanation. He says the person set the fire on שבת by mistake (בשוגג). The next steps explain why someone who acted by mistake is still exempt from paying.

keyTerms.meaning: By mistake, without knowing it was forbidden or that it was שבת

phrases.english: רבא said:
Our משנה is talking about someone who acted by mistake,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second answer, separate from the clever-ox approach, to the challenge against רבי יוחנן in step 1.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Alternative redefinition of the משנה's case (אוקימתא)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה's words 'because he is judged with his life' seemed to mean he was actually liable to death, even though the case looked like one where he did not need the ashes. That contradicts רבי יוחנן.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה is about someone who set the fire by mistake (בשוגג). Steps 12–14 give the full reasoning.

steps.title: Support from the teaching of דבי חזקיה: one who kills a person never pays money
steps.stepSummary: רבא's view is backed by the ברייתא of דבי חזקיה. It compares killing a person to killing an animal. Killing an animal always brings payment, and killing a person never brings payment, whether it was done on purpose or by mistake.
steps.simpleTranslation: This follows what the school of חזקיה taught. The פסוק puts 'one who kills a man' next to 'one who kills an animal.' For killing an animal, the תורה made no difference between a mistake and on purpose, between meaning it and not meaning it, or between a blow on the way down and a blow on the way up. In every case he pays. So too for killing a person, make no difference between these cases. In every case he does not pay money.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to support רבא's idea that a person can be exempt from paying even when he acted by mistake.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא learns from the פסוק that killing a person and killing an animal follow parallel rules, but with opposite results. Killing an animal always means paying. Killing a person never means paying money, even when it was unintentional and there is no actual death penalty. So the exemption depends on the kind of act, not on whether he actually gets executed.

keyTerms.meaning: The school of חזקיה, the source of this ברייתא
A blow on the way down / a blow on the way up
To free him from paying money

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the source for the rule that an act of the death-penalty type frees a person from paying money, even when it was done unintentionally.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not read the ברייתא as saying the two cases have the same outcome. They share the same idea, that intent makes no difference, but the results are opposite: for an animal he always pays, and for a person he never pays money.

phrases.english: And this follows what the school of חזקיה taught,
as the school of חזקיה taught:
'One who kills a man' and 'one who kills an animal' (are compared);
just as with one who kills an animal,

phrases.aramaic: לֹא חִלַּקְתָּ בָּהּ בֵּין שׁוֹגֵג בֵּין מֵזִיד,
phrases.english: you made no difference between by mistake and on purpose,
between meaning to and not meaning to,
between on the way down and on the way up,
phrases.notes: Picture a hand swinging: it can hit as it comes down or as it is being raised up.

phrases.english: not to free him from money but to make him pay money;
so too with one who kills a man,

phrases.aramaic: לֹא תַּחְלוֹק בּוֹ בֵּין שׁוֹגֵג לְמֵזִיד,
phrases.english: do not make a difference between by mistake and on purpose,
between meaning to and not meaning to,
between on the way down and on the way up,
not to make him pay money but to free him from money.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Backs up רבא's reading from Step 11 that the משנה's fire-on-שבת case is one done by mistake.
steps.raayaObject: רבא's claim that someone who acts unintentionally can still be exempt from paying because his act is of the death-penalty type.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא of דבי חזקיה, based on ויקרא 24:21, comparing one who kills a person to one who kills an animal.

steps.title: The חכמים object: the משנה's reason sounds like it fits only an intentional act
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים ask רבא how the משנה could be about a mistake when it says the person is exempt 'because he is judged with his life.'
steps.simpleTranslation: The חכמים said to רבא: Can you really explain the משנה as talking about a mistake? But it says he is exempt 'because he is judged with his life'!
steps.whatsHappening: The חכמים challenge רבא's explanation, using the משנה's own wording.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A person only gets the death penalty when he acts on purpose. The משנה's reason, 'because he is judged with his life,' therefore seems to describe an intentional act. That seems to clash with רבא's claim that the case is one done by mistake.

keyTerms.meaning: Can you really set it up (explain the case) as…?
Judged with his life; liable to the death penalty

phrases.english: The Sages said to רבא:
Can you really explain it as a case of a mistake?
But it teaches 'because he is judged with his life'!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ רַבָּנַן לְרָבָא: מִי מָצֵית מוֹקְמַתְּ לַהּ בְּשׁוֹגֵג
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רבא's reading from Steps 11 and 12 using the wording of the משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's claim that the משנה's case is one done by mistake.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה's reason ('judged with his life') only fits an intentional act, because the death penalty requires intent.

steps.title: רבא explains: since on purpose it brings death, by mistake he is also exempt
steps.stepSummary: רבא explains that the משנה means: because this act done on purpose brings the death penalty, the person is exempt from paying even when he did it by mistake. The death-penalty case is one where he needed the ashes.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what the משנה means: since doing it on purpose brings the death penalty (and what is that case? when he needs the ashes), now that he did it by mistake, he is also exempt from paying.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers the challenge by rereading the משנה's reason as describing the type of act, not the actual case in front of us.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Judged with his life' does not mean this particular person will be executed. It means this kind of act brings the death penalty when done on purpose. Following דבי חזקיה, that is enough to free him from paying even when he acted by mistake. רבא adds that burning counts as a death-penalty act only when the person needs the ashes.
steps.whatToRemember: According to רבא, a person is exempt from paying for an act that would bring the death penalty if done on purpose, even when he did it by mistake. For burning on שבת, this applies where he needed the ashes.

phrases.english: This is what it means:
since on purpose he would be judged with his life,
and what is the case? Where he needs its ashes;
now, when it was by mistake, he is exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָכִי קָאָמַר: כֵּיוָן דִּבְמֵזִיד נִדּוֹן בְּנַפְשׁוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the חכמים's challenge from Step 13.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading the משנה's wording: 'judged with his life' describes the kind of act, not the actual sentence in this case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The phrase 'judged with his life' means the person in this case is actually liable to death, so the case must be intentional.
steps.terutzMaskana: The phrase means the act would bring death if done on purpose (where he needs the ashes). Therefore, even when it is done by mistake, he is exempt from paying.

steps.title: An ox chased another ox and the owners disagree about what caused the injury
steps.stepSummary: The new משנה rules that if the injured ox's owner blames the chasing ox and the other owner says a rock caused it, the one who wants to collect must bring proof.
steps.simpleTranslation: An ox was chasing another ox, and the chased ox got hurt. One owner says, 'Your ox hurt mine.' The other says, 'No, it got hurt on a rock.' The one who wants to take money from the other must bring proof.
steps.whatsHappening: A brand new משנה starts here. It gives a case where one ox chased another and the chased ox was hurt, but nobody knows for sure how it happened.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The owner of the hurt ox wants to be paid, but he has no proof that the chasing ox did the damage. The other owner says the ox hurt itself on a rock. The משנה rules that money stays where it is unless the person trying to collect it proves his claim.

keyTerms.meaning: Our משנה, the opening of a new teaching
The one who wants to take money from his fellow must bring proof

steps.whatToRemember: Without proof, the owner of the chasing ox does not pay. The burden is on the person who wants to collect.
steps.whyThisMatters: The rule הַמּוֹצִיא מֵחֲבֵירוֹ עָלָיו הָרְאָיָה is a basic principle of monetary law that comes up all over ש״ס.

phrases.english: MISHNA

phrases.aramaic: שׁוֹר שֶׁהָיָה רוֹדֵף אַחַר שׁוֹר אַחֵר,
phrases.english: An ox that was chasing another ox,
and it was injured;
this one says: "Your ox did the damage,"
phrases.notes: This is the owner of the hurt ox talking to the owner of the chasing ox.

phrases.english: and that one says: "Not so,
rather, it was hurt by a rock" –
the one who takes money from his fellow must bring the proof.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ שׁוֹר שֶׁהָיָה רוֹדֵף אַחַר שׁוֹר אַחֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה after the discussion of fire on שבת and paying for damage is finished.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When it is unclear whether the chasing ox caused the injury, the owner of the hurt ox cannot collect unless he brings proof.

steps.title: Two oxen chased one ox and each owner blames the other
steps.stepSummary: The משנה starts a second case: two oxen chased one ox, and each chasing ox's owner says the other one's ox did the damage. The ruling comes next.
steps.simpleTranslation: If two oxen were chasing one ox, and one owner says, 'Your ox did the damage,' and the other owner says, 'No, your ox did the damage'...

phrases.english: If two were chasing after one,
this one says: "Your ox did the damage,"
and that one says: "Your ox did the damage" –

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the first case by adding a second chasing ox, which makes it harder to know who caused the damage.
